events.description: UK and US embassies evacuate Sanaa on the same day; UK mission to Yemen relocates to Jeddah
Kuwait round of Yemen peace talks comes close to agreement but fails after Houthi flexibility is restrained
Fitton-Brown becomes coordinator of the UN Monitoring Team four months after leaving the Yemen ambassadorship
UNSC resolution 1988 splits a separate Taliban sanctions committee from the 1267 regime to support an Afghan peace process
ISIL presence in Jowzjan (a renegade Taliban faction that declared for ISIL) more or less eradicated by the Taliban
Easter Sunday attacks in Sri Lanka by an ISIL-inspired presence; ISIL senior leadership had no advance knowledge; Baghdadi reacted in an audio annex
ISIL loses its last territory in Syria
UN Monitoring Team 25th report identifies Baghdadi's successor Abu Ibrahim al-Hashimi al-Qurashi as Amir al-Mawla
Al-Mawla designated on the UN 1267 sanctions list
UN Monitoring Team 22nd report (summer 2018) states Saif al-Adel and Abu Muhammad al-Masri are in Iran helping Zawahiri manage al-Qaeda; Iran later tells the team it is not true
US-Taliban agreement signed in Doha; includes discussion of lifting UN sanctions on Taliban officials
UN Monitoring Team report (written end of April 2020) notes al-Qaeda and Taliban met to discuss their relationship after the Doha agreement
AQIM emir Abdelmalek Droukdel killed by French forces with US support
Pensacola attack showing AQAP's residual external-operations capability
1988 committee grants travel-ban exemptions to a list of Taliban negotiators travelling to Doha

key_claims: The UN Monitoring Team estimates more than 10,000 ISIL fighters in Iraq and Syria, and ISKP down from 3,500-4,000 to 2,000-2,200 after setbacks in Jowzjan and eastern Afghanistan.
Baghdadi's successor Abu Ibrahim al-Qurashi was identified by the UN in December 2019 as Amir al-Mawla, a known ISIS ideologue and Baghdadi's de facto deputy who had once been in US custody.
The Taliban continues to treasure its relationship with al-Qaeda after the Doha agreement; its denials of al-Qaeda presence have no credibility, and Akhundzada has not renounced Zawahiri's bayah.
Zawahiri is placed within the Taliban orbit, likely in Afghanistan, communicating with the Taliban particularly via the Haqqani Network; UN sees no indication he died of COVID-19.
Some Taliban constituencies have marriage/family and comrades-in-arms ties to al-Qaeda and have had to be reassured the Taliban will not break with it.
The Haqqani Network, part of the Taliban, is reported to have facilitated or had foreknowledge of some ISIS-claimed attacks, giving the Taliban deniability, even while fighting ISKP elsewhere.
UN 22nd report (2018) placed Saif al-Adel and Abu Muhammad al-Masri in Iran helping Zawahiri manage al-Qaeda's global operations; Iran told the team it was untrue.
The hosts argue Pakistan and Iran have harbored Taliban leadership and networks and supplied weapons and money; the UN is careful about characterizing state relations with the Taliban.
Al-Qaeda's loose, delegated structure under Zawahiri has helped it outlast ISIL; a rumored cross-regional 'Umma Shura' may include regional emirs such as Droukdel, Asim Umar and Wuhayshi.
